---
title: "Bile Secretion and Pathophysiology of Biliary Tract Obstruction"
format: revealjs
---




## Overview

- Bile secretion is one of the major functions of the liver
- Serves two major purposes:
  - Excretion of hepatic metabolites including bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs, and toxins
  - Facilitation of intestinal absorption of lipids and fat-soluble vitamins
- Bile acids have important signaling functions through interaction with gut microbiome
- Through receptor activation, bile acids regulate lipid, glucose, and energy metabolism
- Alterations in bile secretion may contribute to cholelithiasis and its complications
- Obstruction of bile flow results in alterations of coagulation, immune system, and all organ functions

## Bile Secretion: Bile Formation

- Two primary roles of bile in normal physiology:
  - Excretion of organic compounds such as bilirubin and cholesterol
  - Intestinal absorption of lipids
- Bile secretion results from active transport of solutes into the canaliculus
- Followed by passive flow of water
- Water constitutes approximately 85% of the volume of bile
- Major organic solutes in bile:
  - Bilirubin
  - Bile salts
  - Phospholipids
  - Cholesterol

## Bilirubin Metabolism

- Bilirubin is the breakdown product of spent red blood cells
- Conjugated with glucuronic acid by hepatic enzyme glucuronyl transferase
- Excreted actively into the adjacent canaliculus
- Normally, a large enzyme reserve exists to handle excess bilirubin production
- This reserve may be important in hemolytic states

## Bile Salts

- Steroid molecules synthesized by hepatocytes
- Account for approximately 72% of biliary lipids
- Primary bile salts in humans:
  - Cholic acid
  - Chenodeoxycholic acid
- These account for approximately 80% of those produced
- Primary bile salts conjugated with either taurine or glycine
- Can undergo bacterial alteration in intestine to form secondary bile salts:
  - Deoxycholate
  - Lithocholate
- Purpose: solubilize lipids and facilitate their absorption

## Phospholipids and Cholesterol

- Phospholipids:
  - Synthesized in liver in conjunction with bile salt synthesis
  - Account for approximately 24% of biliary lipids
  - Lecithin is primary phospholipid in human bile
  - Constitutes more than 95% of total phospholipids
- Cholesterol:
  - Final major solute of bile
  - Accounts for 4% of lipids
  - Produced primarily by liver with small contribution from dietary sources

## Bile Volume and Flow

- Normal volume of bile secreted daily by liver: 750 to 1000 mL
- Bile flow depends on neurogenic, humoral, and chemical control
- Vagal stimulation increases bile secretion
- Splanchnic stimulation causes vasoconstriction with decreased hepatic blood flow
- Results in diminished bile secretion
- Gastrointestinal hormones that increase bile flow:
  - Secretin
  - Cholecystokinin
  - Gastrin
  - Glucagon
- Most important factor regulating bile volume: rate of bile salt synthesis by hepatocytes

## Bile Composition

- Components of hepatic and gallbladder bile are essentially the same
- Concentration varies considerably due to gallbladder's ability to absorb water
- Gallbladder absorbs water:
  - Actively via sodium-hydrogen (Na+/H+) pumps
  - Passively through aquaporin channels
- Chloride and bicarbonate absorbed by gallbladder epithelium via CFTR
- Secretion of hydrogen ions and absorption of bicarbonate alter acid-base balance
- Hepatic bile is basic; gallbladder bile is acidic

## Table 8.1: Composition of Hepatic and Gallbladder Bile

| CHARACTERISTICS* | HEPATIC BILE | GALLBLADDER BILE |
|-----------------|--------------|------------------|
| Sodium | 160 | 270 |
| Potassium | 5 | 10 |
| Chloride | 90 | 15 |
| Bicarbonate | 45 | 10 |
| Calcium | 4 | 25 |
| Magnesium | 2 | 4 |
| Bilirubin | 1.5 | 15 |
| Proteins | 150 | 200 |
| Bile acids | 50 | 150 |
| Phospholipids | 8 | 40 |
| Cholesterol | 4 | 18 |
| Total solids | — | 125 |
| pH | 7.8 | 7.2 |

*All determinations are milliequivalents per liter, except for pH.

## Gallbladder Absorption

- Gallbladder mucosa absorbs calcium (Ca+2) and magnesium (Mg+2)
- Calcium absorption is not as efficient as sodium and water absorption
- Leads to significantly greater relative increase in calcium concentration in gallbladder
- Bilirubin concentration may be as high as 10-fold
- Precipitation of calcium bilirubinate crystals more likely within gallbladder
- This is major component of pigment gallstones

## Concentration Effects on Biliary Lipids

- Biliary lipids become more concentrated in gallbladder:
  - Bile salts
  - Phospholipids
  - Cholesterol
- Changes occur in capacity of bile to solubilize cholesterol
- Solubility in micellar fraction is increased
- Stability of phospholipid-cholesterol vesicles is greatly decreased
- Cholesterol crystal precipitation occurs preferentially by vesicular mechanisms
- Net effect of concentrating bile: increased tendency to form cholesterol crystals

## Bile Salt Secretion

- Bile secreted from hepatocyte into canaliculi
- Canaliculi drain contents into small bile ducts
- Secretion of bile salts is major osmotic force for generation of bile flow
- Bile acids formed at rate of 500 to 600 mg per day
- Bulk of bile salt pool maintained in:
  - Gallbladder
  - Liver
  - Small intestine
  - Extrahepatic bile ducts

## Bile Acid Synthesis Pathways

- Bile acids synthesized from cholesterol via two main pathways:
  - Classic pathway: leads to formation of cholic acid
  - Alternative pathway: results in synthesis of chenodeoxycholic acid
- Classic pathway is predominant mode in humans
- 60% to 70% of bile acid pool consists of:
  - Cholic acid and its metabolite deoxycholic acid
- Chenodeoxycholic acid occurs less commonly in human bile

## Bile Acid Transport in Plasma

- In plasma, bile acids circulate bound to either albumin or lipoproteins
- In space of Disse within liver, bile salt uptake into hepatocytes is very efficient
- Process mediated by sodium-dependent and sodium-independent mechanisms
- Sodium-dependent pathway:
  - Accounts for more than 80% of taurocholate uptake
  - Less than 50% of cholate uptake
- Transport proteins play key role in this process

## Figure 8.1: Bile Formation in Human Liver

[Figure showing bile formation in human liver with transporters]

- Key transporters identified:
  - NTCP: Sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide
  - OATPs: Organic anion transporting polypeptides
  - BSEP: Bile salt export pump (ABCB11)
  - MRP2: Multidrug-resistance protein-2
  - MDR3: Multidrug-resistance protein 3
  - MRP3: MDR-related protein-3

## Bile Salt Transport Proteins

- Bile salt transporter termed NTCP (sodium-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide)
- Exclusively expressed in liver
- Located in basolateral membrane of hepatocyte
- Sodium-independent hepatic uptake mediated primarily by OATPs
- OATP-C is major sodium-independent bile salt uptake system
- OATP-A also takes up bile acids
- OATP-8 mediates taurocholate uptake

## Intracellular Bile Acid Transport

- Occurs within a matter of seconds
- Two mechanisms responsible for bile acid transcellular movement:
  - Transfer of bile acids from basolateral membrane to canalicular membrane via bile acid-binding proteins
  - Movement of cellular bile salts through vesicular transport
- Transport across canalicular membrane represents rate-limiting step
- Bile salt concentrations are 1,000-fold greater within canalicular than in hepatocytes
- This gradient necessitates active transport mechanism
- ATP-dependent process

## ATP-Binding Cassette Transporters

- ABCB11 (formerly BSEP) plays key role in bile salt transport
- ABC transporters mediate transport of:
  - Metabolites
  - Peptides
  - Fatty acids
  - Cholesterol
  - Lipids
  - Drugs
- Found in liver, intestines, pancreas, lungs, kidneys, brain, macrophages
- MRP2 also transports sulfated and glucuronidated bile salts
- MRP2 mediates export of other organic anions

## Bile Acids as Signaling Molecules

- Recent studies suggest bile acids regulate lipid, glucose, and energy metabolism
- Function mediated primarily by:
  - Nuclear receptor farnesoid X receptor (FXR)
  - G-protein-coupled receptor TGR5
- Bile acids in small and large intestine regulate gut microbiome
- Regulate incretin secretion
- Regulate production of fibroblast growth factors 15 and 19 (FGF15/FGF19)
- These FGFs modulate lipid, glucose, and energy metabolism
- May play role in rapid improvement in glycemic control after gastric bypass surgery

## Biliary Lipid Secretion

- Compared with bile salts, biliary lipids play secondary role in bile formation
- Phospholipids and cholesterol formed primarily from:
  - Low-density lipoproteins circulating in plasma
  - De novo synthesis by hepatocytes
- Biliary lipid secretion crucial for:
  - Cholesterol disposal
  - Intestinal absorption of dietary lipids
  - Cytoprotection against bile acid-induced hepatocyte and cholangiocyte injury

## Phospholipid Secretion

- Involves delivery of phospholipids to inner leaflet of canalicular plasma membrane
- MDR3 transporter translocates phospholipids from inner to outer leaflet
- Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3 develops with MDR3 deficiency
- These patients have no phosphatidylcholine in bile
- Therefore do not form mixed micelles with bile salts
- Toxic bile salts injure biliary epithelium
- Results in neonatal cholestasis, cholestasis of pregnancy, and cirrhosis in adults

## Cholesterol Secretion

- Less known about role of transporter proteins in cholesterol secretion
- ABC transporters ABCG5 and ABCG8 involved in elimination of plant sterols
- Cholesterol is highly nonpolar and insoluble in water
- Therefore also insoluble in bile
- Key to maintaining cholesterol in solution: formation of micelles
- Micelles are bile salt-phospholipid-cholesterol complex
- Bile salts are amphipathic compounds
- Contain both hydrophilic and hydrophobic portions
- In aqueous solutions, bile salts orient with hydrophilic portion outward
- Phospholipids incorporated into micellar structure
- Allows cholesterol to be added to hydrophobic central portion

## Figure 8.2: Cholesterol Crystal Nucleation

[Figure showing concentration of bile leads to net transfer of phospholipids and cholesterol from vesicles to micelles]

- Phospholipids transferred more efficiently than cholesterol
- Leads to cholesterol enrichment of remaining (remodeled) vesicles
- Aggregation of these cholesterol-rich vesicles forms multilamellar liquid crystals of cholesterol monohydrate
- In simplest and smallest form, vesicles are unilamellar
- May aggregate, leading to multilamellar vesicles
- In states of excess cholesterol production, large vesicles may exceed capacity to transport cholesterol
- Crystal precipitation may occur

## Bilirubin Secretion

- Heme released at time of degradation of senescent erythrocytes by reticuloendothelial system
- Heme source of approximately 80% to 85% of bilirubin produced daily
- Remaining 15% to 20% derived largely from breakdown of hepatic hemoproteins
- Both enzymatic and non-enzymatic pathways for formation of bilirubin proposed
- Microsomal enzyme heme oxygenase plays major role in initial conversion of heme to biliverdin
- Biliverdin reduced to bilirubin by cytosolic enzyme biliverdin reductase
- In "unconjugated" form, bilirubin has very low solubility
- Bound avidly to plasma proteins, primarily albumin

## Bilirubin Uptake and Conjugation

- Liver is sole organ capable of removing albumin-bilirubin complex from circulation
- Liver converts potentially toxic bilirubin to water-soluble, nontoxic derivatives
- In sinusoidal membrane of hepatocyte, bilirubin taken up by OATP-C
- OATP-C involved with uptake of both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin
- Unconjugated bilirubin also can cross hepatic sinusoidal membranes by diffusion
- In hepatocyte, bilirubin binds to glutathione-S-transferase
- Catalyzed by bilirubin uridine-5'-diphosphate glycosyltransferase
- Forms bilirubin glucuronides
- Mutations in gene encoding bilirubin UDP-glycosyltransferase associated with:
  - Crigler-Najjar syndrome
  - Gilbert syndrome

## Bilirubin Excretion

- Bilirubin glucuronides excreted into bile canaliculus primarily via MRP2
- MRP2 also plays role in transport of:
  - Glucuronidated bile salts
  - Wide spectrum of organic anions
  - Antibiotic ceftriaxone
- MRP3 expressed in basolateral membrane of hepatocytes and cholangiocytes
- Participates in transport of bilirubin monoglucuronide
- MRP3 may prevent intracellular accumulation of conjugated bilirubin, bile salts, and other organic anions in cholestatic situations

## Bile Flow

- Bile ducts, gallbladder, and sphincter of Oddi act in concert to modify, store, and regulate bile flow
- Bile flow primarily driven by bile salt secretion
- During passage through bile ductules, canalicular bile modified by absorption and secretion of electrolytes and water
- Bicarbonate secretion by bile ducts plays important role in bile salt-independent bile flow
- Gastrointestinal hormone secretin increases bile flow
- Primarily by increasing active secretion of chloride-rich fluid by bile ducts
- Bile duct secretion also stimulated by cholecystokinin and gastrin

## Gallbladder Function

- Bile duct epithelium capable of water and electrolyte absorption
- May be of primary importance in storage of bile during fasting in patients who have undergone cholecystectomy
- Main functions of gallbladder:
  - Concentrate and store hepatic bile during fasting state
  - Deliver bile into duodenum in response to meal
- Usual capacity of human gallbladder: about 40 to 50 mL
- Only small fraction of bile produced each day would be stored without gallbladder's remarkable absorptive capacity

## Enterohepatic Circulation

- Provides important negative feedback system on bile salt synthesis
- If recirculation interrupted by resection of terminal ileum or primary ileal disease:
  - Abnormally large losses of bile salts occur
  - Increases bile salt production to maintain normal bile salt pool
- If bile salts lost through external biliary fistula:
  - Increased bile salt synthesis necessary
- Except in unusual circumstances, bile salt synthesis matches losses
- Maintains constant bile salt pool size
- During fasting, approximately 90% of bile acid pool sequestered in gallbladder

## Figure 8.3: Enterohepatic Circulation of Bile Salts

[Figure showing enterohepatic circulation]

- Cholesterol taken up from plasma by liver
- Bile acids synthesized at rate of 0.6 g/24 hr
- Excreted through biliary system into small bowel
- Most bile salts reabsorbed in terminal ileum
- Returned to liver to be extracted and re-extracted
- Total bile salt pool: 2 to 4 g
- Recycles through enterohepatic cycle 6 to 10 times daily
- Only about 600 mg actually excreted into colon

## Enterohepatic Circulation Details

- Bile salts synthesized and conjugated in liver
- Secreted into bile
- Stored temporarily in gallbladder
- Passed from gallbladder into duodenum
- Absorbed throughout small intestine, especially in ileum
- Returned to liver via portal vein
- This cycling referred to as enterohepatic circulation
- Total amount of bile acids in enterohepatic circulation defined as circulating bile pool
- Nearly 95% of bile salts reabsorbed

## Bacterial Modification of Bile Salts

- Bacterial action in colon on primary bile salts:
  - Cholate
  - Chenodeoxycholate
- Results in formation of secondary bile salts:
  - Deoxycholate
  - Lithocholate
- Bile acid signature of individual very dependent on gut microbial modification
- Bacterial enzymes modify primary bile acids through:
  - Deconjugation
  - Dehydrogenation
  - Dehydroxylation
  - Sulfation reactions
- Bile acids restrict bacterial proliferation and overgrowth
- Physiology dramatically altered when bile ducts become obstructed

## Biliary Obstruction: Introduction

- Evaluation and management of patient with biliary obstruction common problem for general surgeon
- Over past 40 years, significant advances made in understanding of:
  - Pathophysiology
  - Diagnosis
  - Management of jaundiced patient
- Advances in perioperative and operative management improved survival
- Obstructive jaundice affects multiple organ systems:
  - Hepatic
  - Renal
  - Cardiovascular
  - Hematologic
  - Immune systems

## Table 8.2: Classification of Jaundice

| DEFECT IN BILIRUBIN METABOLISM | PREDOMINANT HYPERBILIRUBINEMIA | EXAMPLES |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------|
| Increased production | Unconjugated | Congenital hemoglobinopathies, hemolysis, multiple transfusions, sepsis, burns |
| Impaired hepatocyte uptake | Unconjugated | Gilbert disease, drug induced |
| Reduced conjugation | Unconjugated | Neonatal jaundice, Crigler-Najjar syndrome |
| Altered transport and excretion | Conjugated | Hepatitis, cirrhosis, Dubin-Johnson syndrome, Rotor syndrome |
| Biliary obstruction | Conjugated | Choledocholithiasis, benign strictures, chronic pancreatitis, sclerosing cholangitis, periampullary cancer, biliary malignancies |

## Causes of Jaundice

- Jaundice may result from:
  - Increased production of bilirubin
  - Impaired hepatocyte uptake of bilirubin
  - Reduced conjugation of bilirubin
  - Altered transport or excretion of bilirubin into bile canaliculus
  - Obstruction of intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary tree
- Overproduction, impaired uptake, and reduced conjugation lead to predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
- Altered transport and excretion and biliary ductal obstruction result in primarily conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
- Some patients have multiple defects in normal metabolism

## Classification of Bile Duct Obstruction

- Diseases causing bile duct obstruction divided into:
  - Complete obstruction
  - Intermittent obstruction
  - Chronic incomplete obstruction
  - Segmental duct obstruction
- Patients with complete biliary obstruction will have clinical jaundice
- Patients with intermittent obstruction may experience symptoms without clinical jaundice
- Hepatic fibrosis can eventually develop in chronic incomplete obstruction
- Biliary cirrhosis can develop

## Box 8.1: Lesions Commonly Associated With Biliary Tract Obstruction

**Type I: Complete Obstruction**
- Tumors of the head of the pancreas
- Common bile duct ligation
- Cholangiocarcinoma
- Gallbladder cancer
- Parenchymal liver tumors (primary or secondary)

**Type II: Intermittent Obstruction**
- Choledocholithiasis
- Periampullary tumors
- Duodenal diverticula
- Choledochal cyst
- Polycystic liver disease
- Biliary parasites
- Hemobilia

## Box 8.1 (Continued)

**Type III: Chronic Incomplete Obstruction**
- Strictures of the common bile duct
- Congenital biliary atresia
- Traumatic (iatrogenic)
- Sclerosing cholangitis
- Post radiotherapy
- Stenosis of biliary-enteric anastomosis
- Chronic pancreatitis
- Cystic fibrosis
- Sphincter of Oddi stenosis

**Type IV: Segmental Obstruction**
- Traumatic
- Intrahepatic stones
- Sclerosing cholangitis
- Cholangiocarcinoma

## Pathophysiology of Biliary Obstruction

- Biliary obstruction produces local effects on bile ducts
- Leads to derangements of hepatic function
- Ultimately leads to widespread systemic effects
- Jaundiced patients at increased risk for:
  - Hepatic dysfunction
  - Renal failure
  - Cardiovascular impairments
  - Nutritional deficiencies
  - Bleeding problems
  - Infections
  - Wound complications
- Perioperative mortality and morbidity increased in patients with biliary obstruction

## Hepatobiliary Effects

- Hepatocytes arranged in plates along which blood flows from portal to central veins
- Small apical domains of adjacent hepatocytes form tubular lumen (canaliculus)
- Canaliculus is site of primary bile formation
- From canalicular network, bile flows to small ductules and subsequently to larger ducts
- With biliary obstruction:
  - Bile canaliculi become dilated
  - Microvilli are distorted and swollen
- In long-standing obstruction:
  - Intrahepatic bile ductule proliferation occurs
  - Increase in length and tortuosity of canaliculi

## Biliary Pressure Changes

- Biliary system normally has low pressure (5-10 cm H2O)
- In complete or partial biliary obstruction, biliary pressure can approach 30 cm H2O
- As biliary pressure increases:
  - Tight junctions between hepatocytes and bile duct cells disrupted
  - Increase in bile duct and canalicular permeability
- Bile contents can freely reflux into liver sinusoids
- Causes marked polymorphonuclear leukocyte infiltration into portal triads
- Inflammatory response followed by increased fibrinogenesis
- Deposition of reticulin fibers
- Conversion to type I collagen

## Extrahepatic Bile Duct Changes

- Extrahepatic bile ducts exhibit:
  - Mucosal atrophy
  - Squamous metaplasia
- Followed by:
  - Inflammatory infiltration
  - Fibrosis in subepithelial layers of bile duct
- Elevated biliary pressure can alter bile production by hepatocytes
- In setting of biliary obstruction and elevated biliary pressure:
  - Bile becomes less lithogenic
  - Relative decrease in cholesterol and phospholipid secretion compared with bile acid secretion

## Effects of Relief of Obstruction

- With relief of biliary obstruction and normalization of biliary pressures:
  - Recovery of cholesterol and phospholipid secretion more rapid than bile acid secretion
  - Bile is more lithogenic in this setting
- This phenomenon may lead to premature occlusion of decompressive biliary stents
- Several authors reported impairment of macrovascular and microvascular perfusion of liver in obstructive jaundice
- Intravital fluorescence microscopy shown significant increase in number of nonperfused sinusoids after three days of extrahepatic obstruction
- May explain increased risk for hepatocellular dysfunction when performing liver resections in patients with obstructive jaundice

## Hepatic Function Changes

- Extrahepatic biliary obstruction and jaundice can alter important secretory, metabolic, and synthetic functions of liver
- When biliary pressure rises higher than 20 cm H2O:
  - Hepatic bile secretion diminished
  - Hepatocytes cannot excrete efficiently against high pressure
- Excretory products of hepatocytes reflux directly into vascular system
- Leads to systemic toxicity
- Patients with jaundice have decreased capacity to excrete drugs normally secreted into bile
- Increased concentration of bile acids inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
- Decrease in rate of oxidative metabolism in liver

## Hepatocyte Changes

- Bile acids in abnormally high concentrations can induce apoptosis in hepatocytes
- Synthetic function of hepatocyte also decreased with obstructive jaundice
- Evidenced by decreased plasma levels of:
  - Albumin
  - Clotting factors
  - Secretory immunoglobulins (IgA)
- Kupffer cells are tissue macrophages
- Predominant cell type of hepatic reticuloendothelial system
- Normally filter infectious agents, damaged blood cells, cellular debris, fibrin degradation products, and endotoxin
- Obstructive jaundice has profound effects on Kupffer cells

## Kupffer Cell Effects

- Decreased endocytosis
- Decreased phagocytosis
- Decreased clearance of bacteria and endotoxin
- Decreased expression of major histocompatibility complex class II antigen
- Diminished ability to process antigen
- Biliary obstruction increases levels of proinflammatory cytokines:
  - Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α
  - Interleukin (IL)-6

## Cardiovascular Effects

- Obstructive jaundice may cause severe hemodynamic and cardiac disturbances
- Experimental animals with obstructive jaundice tend to be hypotensive
- Exhibit exaggerated hypotensive response to hemorrhage
- Studies demonstrated bile duct ligation:
  - Decreases cardiac contractility
  - Reduces left ventricular pressures
  - Impairs response to β agonist drugs
  - Decreases peripheral vascular resistance
- Negative correlation between serum bilirubin and left ventricular systolic work
- Successful internal biliary drainage associated with significant increase in cardiac output, compliance, and contractility

## Cardiovascular Effects (Continued)

- Combination of depressed cardiac function and decreased total peripheral resistance
- Makes jaundiced patient more susceptible to development of postoperative shock
- Than nonjaundiced patients

## Renal Effects

- Association between jaundice and postoperative renal failure known for many years
- Reported incidence of postoperative acute kidney injury as high as 10%
- Varies depending on nature of procedure
- Mortality rate in patients with jaundice who develop renal failure reported as high as 70%
- Important factors in development of renal failure:
  - Depressed cardiac function
  - Hypovolemia
  - Bile salt-mediated effects on renal FXR and TGR5 receptors
  - Endotoxemia

## Renal Effects (Continued)

- Decreased cardiac function leads to decrease in renal perfusion
- Decreased cardiac output may result in stretching of atrium
- Increased production of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)
- ANP causes:
  - Natriuresis
  - Counters action of water- and sodium-retaining hormones
  - Inhibits thirst mechanism
  - Produces peripheral vasodilation
- Plasma levels of ANP increased in experimental animals and patients with extrahepatic biliary obstruction

## Renal Effects of Bile Acids

- Increased serum levels of bile acids have direct diuretic and natriuretic effect on kidney
- Results in significant extracellular volume depletion and hypovolemia
- Infusion of bile into renal artery of dogs results in:
  - Increased urine flow
  - Natriuresis
  - Kaliuresis
- Diuretic effect may be mediated by increased prostaglandin E2 production by kidney
- And/or by effect on FXR and TGR5 receptors

## Endotoxemia and Renal Failure

- Approximately 50% of patients with obstructive jaundice have endotoxin in peripheral blood
- May be result of:
  - Decreased hepatic clearance of endotoxin by Kupffer cells
  - Lack of bile salts in gut lumen
- Bile salts normally prevent absorption of endotoxins
- Bile salts normally inhibit anaerobic bacterial growth
- Endotoxin causes:
  - Renal vasoconstriction
  - Redistribution of renal blood flow away from cortex
  - Disturbances in coagulation
  - Activation of complement, macrophages, leukocytes, and platelets
- Glomerular and peritubular fibrin deposited
- Combined with reduced renal cortical blood flow
- Results in tubular and cortical necrosis

## Figure 8.4: Obstructive Jaundice Leads to Renal Impairment

[Figure showing pathways from obstructive jaundice to renal impairment]

- Obstructive jaundice leads to:
  - Decreased Kupffer cell clearance
  - Increased systemic bile salts
  - Decreased gut bile salts
  - Increased systemic bilirubin
- These lead to endotoxemia
- Endotoxemia affects cardiovascular, renal, and coagulation systems
- Ultimately leads to renal impairment or acute renal failure

## Coagulation Effects

- Disturbances of blood coagulation commonly present in jaundiced patients
- Most frequently observed abnormality: prolongation of prothrombin time
- Results from impaired vitamin K absorption from gut
- Secondary to lack of intestinal bile
- Coagulopathy usually reversible with parenteral administration of vitamin K
- Decreased bile levels in small intestine may result in diminished absorption of other fat-soluble vitamins and fats
- Results in weight loss and loss of calcium
- May further contribute to clotting abnormalities

## Coagulation Effects (Continued)

- In experimental animals, endotoxin affects metabolism of factors XI and XII
- Causes platelet and direct endothelial damage
- Endotoxin release in patients with jaundice results in low-grade disseminated intravascular coagulation
- Increased fibrin degradation products
- Patients with jaundice with circulating endotoxin or increased fibrin degradation product levels before surgery at increased risk for hemorrhagic complications
- Patients with coexisting cirrhosis often have additional problems:
  - Thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism
  - Fibrinolysis
- Portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis exacerbates coagulation disorders

## Immune System Effects

- Surgery in patients with jaundice associated with higher rate of postoperative septic complications
- Due in large measure to defects in cellular immunity
- Makes them more prone to infection
- Association between jaundice and altered delayed-type hypersensitivity
- Only 16% of 118 patients with jaundice were immunocompetent
- Compared with 76% of 59 healthy controls
- Tested with panel of seven skin antigens
- Ability of reticuloendothelial system to clear bacteria and endotoxin reduced in obstructive jaundice

## Immune System Effects (Continued)

- Studies in humans demonstrated:
  - Decreased T-lymphocyte proliferation
  - Decreased expression of adhesion molecules
  - Altered monocyte functions
- Septic manifestations in jaundiced patients result from cellular immune insufficiency
- Induced by release of cytokines:
  - TNF-α
  - IL-1
  - IL-6
  - Interferon-γ
- Prostaglandins and other inflammatory mediators also involved

## Bacterial Translocation

- Absence of bile from intestinal tract plays role in infectious complications
- Bacterial translocation from gut increased in setting of bile duct obstruction
- Obstruction causes disruption of enterohepatic circulation
- Results in loss of emulsifying antientotoxin effect of bile acids
- Larger pool of endotoxin available within intestine for absorption into portal circulation
- Combination of reduced or absent bile in intestine and impaired cellular immunity and reticuloendothelial cell function
- Major factor contributing to more frequent infective complications

## Acute Cholangitis

- Bacterial infection of biliary ductal system
- Varies in severity from mild and self-limited to severe and life threatening
- Clinical triad associated with cholangitis first described in 1877 by Charcot:
  - Fever
  - Jaundice
  - Pain
- Cholangitis results from combination of two factors:
  - Significant bacterial concentrations in bile
  - Biliary obstruction

## Cholangitis Pathophysiology

- Bile from gallbladder and bile ducts usually sterile
- In presence of common bile duct stones or other obstructing pathology, incidence of positive cultures increases
- Instrumentation of biliary tree greatly increases rates of bile colonization
- Most common organisms recovered from bile in patients with cholangitis:
  - Escherichia coli
  - Klebsiella pneumoniae
  - Enterococci
  - Bacteroides fragilis
- Even in presence of high biliary bacterial concentrations, clinical cholangitis and bacteremia will not develop unless obstruction causes elevated intraductal pressures

## Cholangitis and Biliary Pressure

- Normal biliary pressures range from 7 to 14 cm H2O
- In presence of bacteribilia and normal biliary pressures, hepatic venous blood and perihepatic lymph are sterile
- With partial or complete biliary obstruction, intrabiliary pressures rise to 20 to 30 cm H2O
- Organisms rapidly appear in both blood and lymph
- Fever and chills associated with cholangitis result from systemic bacteremia
- Caused by cholangiovenous and cholangiolymphatic reflux

## Causes of Biliary Obstruction

- Most common causes:
  - Choledocholithiasis
  - Benign strictures
  - Biliary-enteric anastomotic strictures
  - Periampullary or proximal biliary cancers
- Before 1980, choledocholithiasis cause of approximately 80% of reported cases of cholangitis
- In recent years, malignant strictures have become frequent cause
- Especially after placement of biliary stents
- Endoscopic cholangiography, percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography, and stent placement known to cause bacteremia
- Frequently performed in patients with presumptive diagnosis of malignant obstruction

## Wound Healing Effects

- Delayed wound healing and high incidence of wound dehiscence and incisional hernia observed in patients with jaundice undergoing surgery
- Patients with obstructive jaundice have decreased activity of enzyme propyl hydroxylase in skin
- Propyl hydroxylase necessary for incorporation of amino acid proline into collagen
- Activity used as measure of collagen synthesis
- Patients with jaundice had only 11% of skin propyl hydroxylase activity of controls
- In subgroup with jaundice secondary to malignancy, activity less than 7% of controls

## Wound Healing Effects (Continued)

- With relief of obstruction, activity increased to 22% of controls
- In patients with jaundice secondary to benign obstruction, activity increased to 100% of controls

## Other Factors: Nutrition

- Other problems facing patients with jaundice:
  - Anorexia
  - Weight loss
  - Malnutrition
- Appetite adversely influenced by lack of bile salts in intestinal tract
- Patients with pancreatic or periampullary malignant lesions may have:
  - Partial duodenal obstruction
  - Abnormal gastric emptying
  - Tumor infiltration of celiac nerve plexus
- Patients with pancreatic or ampullary tumors may have pancreatic endocrine and exocrine insufficiency
- May further compound other nutritional defects
- May exacerbate immune deficits

## Prolonged Effects of Obstructive Jaundice

- Several recent observations suggest many physiologic derangements induced by obstructive jaundice take long time to reverse
- Hepatic mitochondrial function does not return to normal even seven weeks after relief of obstruction
- Same prolonged effect noted with:
  - Lymphocyte function
  - Polymorphonuclear function
  - Kupffer cell function
- Even patients who have had temporary relief of biliary obstruction via percutaneous or endoscopic stents likely to remain at risk for significant complications after surgery
- Derangements in hepatic function likely still present at time of operation
- Preoperative jaundice may adversely affect long-term survival in patients with resected pancreatic cancer

## Management: Introduction

- Historically, only option for relief of obstructive jaundice was operative intervention
- With development of therapeutic techniques, many nonoperative options now available:
  - Percutaneous stenting
  - Endoscopic stenting
  - Balloon dilation
  - Endoscopic sphincterotomy
- Surgeon must determine safest and most effective therapy for each individual patient
- Must adequately prepare each patient for surgery or nonoperative therapeutic intervention

## Management: General Considerations

- Patients with obstructive jaundice and those with hepatocellular disease severe enough to cause jaundice prone to many secondary problems
- Patients with jaundice at increased risk for:
  - Kidney injury
  - Gastrointestinal bleeding
  - Infections
  - Wound complications
- Cardiac, pulmonary, and renal function must be considered in every patient undergoing major abdominal surgery
- Special attention must be focused on:
  - Nutritional status
  - Coagulability
  - Immune function
  - Presence or absence of biliary sepsis
- Complications related to portal hypertension may develop in patients with chronic liver disease and cirrhosis

## Cardiopulmonary Assessment

- In assessing cardiopulmonary status, consider:
  - Patient's age
  - History of recent myocardial infarction
  - Presence of congestive heart failure
  - Significant valvular heart disease
  - Disturbance of normal cardiac rhythm
- All have been correlated with increased operative risk
- Patients with severe pulmonary disease may not be candidates for extensive abdominal surgery

## Renal Assessment

- Patients with jaundice, especially those with cirrhosis and cholangitis, at increased risk for renal insufficiency
- Maintenance of adequate blood volume and correction of dehydration extremely important to avoid renal complications
- Fluid management can be quite complex in patients with jaundice
- Both excess and insufficient fluids may be problematic
- Selected patients may benefit from invasive hemodynamic monitoring
- To assist with goal-directed fluid management

## Prevention of Renal Complications

- Certain oral bile salts shown to be efficacious in preventing development of postoperative kidney injury
- In one study, 54% of 24 patients with jaundice not given oral bile salts before surgery found to have systemic endotoxemia
- Associated with renal impairment in two-thirds of cases
- In comparison, none of eight patients with jaundice given 500 mg of sodium deoxycholate every eight hours for 48 hours before surgery had portal or systemic endotoxemia
- None of these eight patients had evidence of renal impairment

## Nutritional Assessment and Support

- Malnutrition is significant risk factor for surgery in setting of obstructive jaundice
- Patients who died in postoperative period after surgery for obstructive jaundice had significant reduction in:
  - Body weight
  - Midarm circumference
  - Total body potassium
  - Reactivity to skin test antigens preoperatively
- Enteral hyperalimentation found to significantly decrease operative morbidity and mortality
- In group treated with 20 days of preoperative percutaneous biliary drainage
- Most patients with benign biliary problems adequately nourished
- Various degrees of malnutrition frequently present in patients with malignant obstruction
- Patients with malignant obstructive jaundice should be evaluated for malnutrition
- Nutritional support instituted if necessary

## Coagulation Management

- Patients with obstructive jaundice, cholangitis, or cirrhosis all prone to excessive intraoperative bleeding
- Most common clotting defect in patients with obstructive jaundice: prolongation of prothrombin time (PT)
- Usually reversible by administration of parenteral vitamin K
- Patients with severe jaundice and/or cholangitis also may develop disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
- May require infusion of platelets and fresh frozen plasma
- Reversal of DIC also requires control of underlying sepsis
- Should include biliary drainage in patients with cholangitis
- In addition to systemic antibiotics

## Coagulation Management in Cirrhotic Patients

- Clotting abnormalities often multifactorial:
  - Thrombocytopenia secondary to hypersplenism
  - Prolongation of PT and partial thromboplastin time (PTT)
  - Fibrinolysis
- Vitamin K should be administered if PT is prolonged
- If no effect seen and/or if PTT also prolonged, fresh frozen plasma should be given
- Thrombocytopenia usually can be managed by intraoperative platelet infusions
- If patient has shortened clot lysis time and hypofibrinogenemia, ε-aminocaproic acid may be indicated

## Pruritus Management

- Pruritus often distressing problem in jaundiced patient
- Exact cause remains obscure
- Increased circulating levels of bile salts, histamines, and central nervous system opiate receptors implicated
- In some patients, relief from itching obtained by bile salt-binding agents such as cholestyramine
- Various sedatives and antihistamines also can provide relief
- Relief of biliary obstruction remains most effective method for managing pruritus
- Improvement can occur rapidly after stent placement
- Occasionally can take a week or so

## Cholangitis Management

- Biliary sepsis identified as major risk in jaundiced patients
- Cholangitis occurs when partial or complete obstruction of bile duct exists
- Results in increased intraluminal pressure and infected bile proximal to obstruction
- Patients with cholangitis may present with:
  - Right upper quadrant abdominal pain
  - Fever
  - Jaundice (Charcot's triad)
- Patients with "toxic" cholangitis have Charcot's triad plus:
  - Shock
  - Mental confusion (Reynold's pentad)
- Have significant mortality with appropriate antibiotic therapy alone
- Require emergent biliary decompression

## Indications for Urgent Biliary Decompression

- Gigot and associates identified seven prognostic factors as indications for urgent biliary decompression:
  1. Acute kidney injury
  2. Liver abscess
  3. Cirrhosis
  4. High malignant stricture
  5. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography
  6. Female gender
  7. Advanced age
- Emergent surgical treatment associated with significant morbidity and mortality
- Both percutaneous and endoscopic biliary drainage proposed as effective therapy
- For the 5% to 10% of patients with cholangitis unresponsive to conservative therapy
- Endoscopic drainage associated with lower morbidity (34% vs. 66%) and mortality (10% vs. 32%) than operative drainage

## Preoperative Drainage

- Preoperative relief of jaundice and reversal of systemic effects by endoscopic or transhepatic biliary decompression proposed as method to decrease risk of surgery
- However, several prospective randomized studies shown routine use of preoperative biliary drainage (PBD) does not reduce operative morbidity or mortality
- Meta-analyses concluded PBD increased (P < .001) rather than decreased overall complications from surgery
- Drainage procedure provided no benefit in terms of reduced mortality or decreased hospital stay
- Insufficient evidence exists to determine whether endoscopic plastic or metal stents or percutaneous transhepatic drains are better than no drainage
- EUS-guided biliary drainage may have advantage over percutaneous drainage when ERCP fails

## Preoperative Drainage: Additional Considerations

- Criticism of some prospective studies: duration of preoperative drainage (10-18 days) may have been inadequate
- To reverse multiple metabolic and immunologic abnormalities associated with severe obstructive jaundice
- Both animal and human studies demonstrate recovery of various metabolic and immune functions requires at least six weeks
- Animal studies strongly suggest return of bile to intestinal tract has significant advantages over external biliary drainage
- Although data suggest routine PBD may be of limited benefit, PBD may have value in selected patients with:
  - Advanced malnutrition
  - Biliary sepsis
  - Hilar malignancies that require liver resection

## Preoperative Drainage: Specific Indications

- Most published data regarding PBD focus on patients with periampullary malignancy
- Patients with proximal biliary obstruction undergoing major hepatic resection represent entirely different subgroup
- Multicenter European study suggests those requiring right hepatectomy benefit from preoperative drainage of future liver remnant
- In patients with perihilar cholangiocarcinoma:
  - Percutaneous drainage associated with less cholangitis and pancreatitis compared with endoscopic drainage
- Preoperatively placed transhepatic catheters may be of value in operating room during difficult biliary dissections
- May aid in placement of long-term transhepatic stents
- Preoperative drainage required in patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy
- Metal stents have fewer problems with cholangitis at no additional cost
- Plastic stents preferable for patients with hilar cholangiocarcinoma in whom surgery is planned

## Summary

- Over past few decades, tremendous strides made in understanding of bile secretion and ability to care for jaundiced patient
- Clinicians now have better understanding of:
  - Normal bile salt physiology
  - Biliary lipid physiology
  - Bilirubin physiology
- Can classify diseases that cause jaundice as defects in normal metabolism
- Investigators have elucidated multiple pathophysiologic effects of jaundice
- Explain why jaundiced patients at risk for increased perioperative morbidity and mortality

## Key Points: Bile Secretion

- Bile secretion is major function of liver
- Two primary roles: excretion of organic compounds and intestinal absorption of lipids
- Water constitutes approximately 85% of bile volume
- Major organic solutes: bilirubin, bile salts, phospholipids, cholesterol
- Bile salts account for approximately 72% of biliary lipids
- Phospholipids account for approximately 24% of biliary lipids
- Cholesterol accounts for 4% of biliary lipids
- Normal volume of bile secreted daily: 750 to 1000 mL

## Key Points: Bile Composition

- Hepatic and gallbladder bile have same components but different concentrations
- Gallbladder absorbs water, sodium, chloride, bicarbonate
- Gallbladder mucosa also absorbs calcium and magnesium
- Calcium absorption less efficient than sodium and water
- Leads to greater relative increase in calcium concentration
- Bilirubin concentration may be as high as 10-fold
- Precipitation of calcium bilirubinate crystals more likely in gallbladder

## Key Points: Bile Salt Transport

- Bile salt transporter NTCP exclusively expressed in liver
- Located in basolateral membrane of hepatocyte
- Sodium-independent hepatic uptake mediated primarily by OATPs
- OATP-C is major sodium-independent bile salt uptake system
- Transport across canalicular membrane is rate-limiting step
- Bile salt concentrations 1,000-fold greater within canalicular than in hepatocytes
- ATP-dependent process
- ABCB11 (BSEP) plays key role

## Key Points: Enterohepatic Circulation

- Bile salts synthesized and conjugated in liver
- Secreted into bile
- Stored temporarily in gallbladder
- Passed into duodenum
- Absorbed throughout small intestine, especially ileum
- Returned to liver via portal vein
- Total bile salt pool: 2 to 4 g
- Recycles 6 to 10 times daily
- Only about 600 mg excreted into colon
- Nearly 95% of bile salts reabsorbed

## Key Points: Biliary Obstruction Effects

- Affects multiple organ systems:
  - Hepatic
  - Renal
  - Cardiovascular
  - Hematologic
  - Immune
- Jaundiced patients at increased risk for:
  - Hepatic dysfunction
  - Renal failure
  - Cardiovascular impairments
  - Nutritional deficiencies
  - Bleeding problems
  - Infections
  - Wound complications
- Perioperative mortality and morbidity increased

## Key Points: Hepatobiliary Effects

- Bile canaliculi become dilated
- Microvilli distorted and swollen
- Intrahepatic bile ductule proliferation in long-standing obstruction
- Biliary pressure can approach 30 cm H2O
- Tight junctions disrupted
- Bile contents reflux into liver sinusoids
- Inflammatory response with fibrinogenesis
- Extrahepatic bile ducts exhibit mucosal atrophy and squamous metaplasia

## Key Points: Cardiovascular Effects

- Obstructive jaundice causes hemodynamic and cardiac disturbances
- Bile duct ligation:
  - Decreases cardiac contractility
  - Reduces left ventricular pressures
  - Impairs response to β agonist drugs
  - Decreases peripheral vascular resistance
- Negative correlation between serum bilirubin and left ventricular systolic work
- Internal biliary drainage associated with increased cardiac output, compliance, and contractility
- Jaundiced patient more susceptible to postoperative shock

## Key Points: Renal Effects

- Postoperative acute kidney injury incidence as high as 10%
- Mortality rate in patients with jaundice who develop renal failure as high as 70%
- Factors in development of renal failure:
  - Depressed cardiac function
  - Hypovolemia
  - Bile salt-mediated effects on renal FXR and TGR5 receptors
  - Endotoxemia
- Approximately 50% of patients with obstructive jaundice have endotoxin in peripheral blood
- Endotoxin causes renal vasoconstriction and redistribution of renal blood flow

## Key Points: Coagulation Effects

- Most frequently observed abnormality: prolongation of prothrombin time
- Results from impaired vitamin K absorption
- Usually reversible with parenteral vitamin K
- Endotoxin release results in low-grade disseminated intravascular coagulation
- Increased fibrin degradation products
- Patients with circulating endotoxin or increased fibrin degradation products at increased risk for hemorrhagic complications
- Patients with coexisting cirrhosis have additional problems

## Key Points: Immune System Effects

- Surgery in patients with jaundice associated with higher rate of postoperative septic complications
- Defects in cellular immunity make them more prone to infection
- Only 16% of patients with jaundice immunocompetent vs. 76% of controls
- Decreased T-lymphocyte proliferation
- Decreased expression of adhesion molecules
- Altered monocyte functions
- Bacterial translocation from gut increased in bile duct obstruction
- Loss of emulsifying antientotoxin effect of bile acids

## Key Points: Cholangitis

- Bacterial infection of biliary ductal system
- Charcot's triad: fever, jaundice, pain
- Results from bacterial concentrations in bile and biliary obstruction
- Most common organisms:
  - Escherichia coli
  - Klebsiella pneumoniae
  - Enterococci
  - Bacteroides fragilis
- Clinical cholangitis and bacteremia will not develop unless obstruction causes elevated intraductal pressures
- Normal biliary pressures: 7 to 14 cm H2O
- With obstruction, pressures rise to 20 to 30 cm H2O
- Organisms rapidly appear in blood and lymph

## Key Points: Wound Healing

- Delayed wound healing and high incidence of wound dehiscence and incisional hernia
- Decreased activity of propyl hydroxylase in skin
- Propyl hydroxylase necessary for incorporation of proline into collagen
- Patients with jaundice had only 11% of skin propyl hydroxylase activity of controls
- In patients with jaundice secondary to malignancy, activity less than 7% of controls
- With relief of obstruction, activity increased to 22% of controls
- In patients with benign obstruction, activity increased to 100% of controls

## Key Points: Management

- Many nonoperative options now available for relief of obstructive jaundice:
  - Percutaneous stenting
  - Endoscopic stenting
  - Balloon dilation
  - Endoscopic sphincterotomy
- Surgeon must determine safest and most effective therapy for each patient
- Special attention to:
  - Nutritional status
  - Coagulability
  - Immune function
  - Presence or absence of biliary sepsis
- Routine preoperative biliary drainage does not reduce operative morbidity or mortality
- May have value in selected patients

## Key Points: Preoperative Drainage

- Several prospective randomized studies shown routine PBD does not reduce operative morbidity or mortality
- Meta-analyses concluded PBD increased overall complications from surgery
- No benefit in terms of reduced mortality or decreased hospital stay
- PBD may have value in selected patients with:
  - Advanced malnutrition
  - Biliary sepsis
  - Hilar malignancies requiring liver resection
- Preoperative drainage required in patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy
- Metal stents have fewer problems with cholangitis
- Plastic stents preferable for patients with hilar cholangiocarcinoma in whom surgery is planned

## Conclusion

- Tremendous strides made in understanding bile secretion and care of jaundiced patient
- Better understanding of normal bile salt, biliary lipid, and bilirubin physiology
- Can classify diseases that cause jaundice as defects in normal metabolism
- Multiple pathophysiologic effects of jaundice elucidated
- Explain why jaundiced patients at risk for increased perioperative morbidity and mortality
- Management requires careful assessment of multiple organ systems
- Selection of appropriate therapeutic interventions based on individual patient characteristics
